claims_disputed.claim: Maintenance concentrates early and more often touches frontmatter than the instruction body
claims_disputed.reason: The 'concentrates early' half is the reading the paper explicitly warns against. Only size-normalized churn drops (31.2 -> 5.6 per 100 lines, month 1 to 2). The share of project commits touching these workflows shows no significant month-to-month change (all adjusted p >= .561, Fig. 6b), and §IV-B says the churn drop 'should not be taken as evidence that workflow maintenance declines independently of overall project activity'. The 78.2%-updated-in-month-4 figure appears only in the abstract, intro and discussion, never in the RQ2 results text. It is also partly built in by the selection rule (first-to-last observed change >= 120 days). The frontmatter half holds: project medians are 74.5% vs 50.0%, and pooled it is 62.1% vs 55.1% once both-region edits are counted in each.

missed_issues: Methodology field says 'Wilcoxon-type test for churn'. The paper uses project-paired sign tests with Holm correction across 12 comparisons (§IV-B).

The RQ4 kappa of 0.715 pools every file-label pair, including labels absent from both prediction and reference. Per-label reliability is uneven: Domain Context is kappa 0.414 with 83 false positives, Rule Conformance 0.447 (Table V). 'Reliably' holds in aggregate, not for every label.

The RQ2 cohort (348 files, 43 projects) is selected on a >= 120-day first-to-last-change span, which guarantees ongoing edits. The selection effect is broader than survivorship of files, and it inflates any 'still maintained' rate.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with every score. The P36 neutral stance is right: the paper counts how often prose step orders and branches appear (88.2% / 87.2%) but never compares an enforced graph against prose or an open loop. The applicability text's 'cheap middle ground' framing is the reviewer's inference, not a finding. The one disputed claim conflates normalized-churn decline with maintenance decline, which the authors themselves rule out.
